newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook- Summer gasoline heating up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook- Summer gasoline heating up.

text.p: Gasoline trade should dominate market activity this week, with steady summer demand bolstering prompt barrel differentials on the Gulf Coast, Midcontinent and New York Harbor recently.

The Independence Day holiday, which shortened trading activity last week, is viewed by many players as the peak demand period in the summer driving season, though recent gains in prices could indicate that more bullish movement is likely.
"It's not over yet for the gasoline by a long shot," one trader said. "I think every market dip is a buy."
Distillate trade, however, was expected to be subdued, with high refinery output seen as more than adequate for immediate needs, traders said.
U.S. GULF
Gasoline demand should keep differentials firm for the foreseeable future, according to market traders, keeping pace with the hefty refinery output.
Gulf Coast gasoline prices peaked in mid-November last year at about 69.81 cents a gallon and have trended lower since then, reaching a bottom at 52.13 cents in late June.
However, prices have rebounded more than 5.00 cents since reaching that bottom, aided largely by the strong U.S. demand.
Refinery utilization sat at 96.9 percent of capacity in the latest American Petroleum Institute weekly report, well above the 94.3 percent recorded for the same period last year.
Regular conventional M1 gasoline continues to see brisk buying on the Colonial Pipeline scheduling deadlines, including the front 20th cycle, which hits at the end of Monday.
Prompt M1 barrels were talked at about 0.85 cents under the August NYMEX futures early Monday, a gain of nearly 1.00 cent from the level seen before the Independence Day holiday.
Renewed buying in the reformulated A1 gasoline is expected to continue this week, with prompt barrels seen at a 2.50-cent premium to the M1 gasoline, or about 1.75 cents above the August NYMEX.
MIDCONTINENT
Traders in the Midcontinent had mixed forecasts for gasoline's performance this week but were unanimous that activity would be relatively quiet.

"The Gulf Coast is rallying so that should help push up the Midcontinent," said a Group Three player. He added the hub appeared to be carrying shorts in the market, which could cause an increase in differentials.
"There is just more buying than selling. It's as simple as that," he said.
But other players pointed out that arbitrage opportunities remain open for the Gulf Coast as strength in the Midcontinent continues to pull barrels up. The profit margin is about one cent.
The impact of bringing up more barrels into the Midcontinent will add to an already ample supply and possibly weaken gasoline's value, traders said.

"There are no problems with gasoline supply right now. I don't expect demand to be that strong to soak up extra barrels," said a Midcontinent trader, adding what is traditionally the highest gasoline demand weekend has passed.
In quiet Monday activity, prompt unleaded July gasoline differentials eased about a half cent to between 1.75 cents and 2.00 cents a gallon. The any months were unchanged at 0.75/1.00 cent.
NEW YORK HARBOR
Activity in the NYH has been fairly steady in the past few weeks, with an amply-supplied market preventing any sharp movements in differentials.
However, regular conventional M2 gasoline differentials firmed last week, possibly aided by the drop off in imports from Europe as well as the steady U.S. demand.
U.S. gasoline imports totaled 298,000 barrels a day in the latest API data, nearly 300,000 barrels below the previous week's figure.
